text: In the village of Keba Kunda, on the south bank of the Gambia River, there lived a Fula herdsman named Demba.
Demba had tended cattle since he was old enough to walk behind them.

He knew each animal by name — not the short names that strangers give to livestock, but the long names, the names that describe a particular way of holding the head, or a preferred patch of grazing ground, or the memory of a calf born in the rain.
To a stranger, this might sound like property.
But to a Fula herdsman, cattle are something closer to family.
When a man's herd is large and well-kept, people look at him and see a man who knows how to be patient — who rises before dawn and does not complain and provides for what depends on him.
Cattle, in the Fula world, are the physical form of Pulaaku.
And Demba's cattle were the finest in three villages.
